title.en: Sutures, needles, knots, and wound closure

intro.en: Comprehensive guide to surgical suture materials, needle configurations, knot tying techniques, mechanical stapling devices, and prosthetic meshes tested in practical surgery examinations.

items.summary: A natural absorbable monofilament suture derived from mammalian collagen that undergoes rapid enzymatic degradation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Translucent yellowish-amber or straw-coloured strand.
Packaged wet in a conditioning fluid containing alcohol and water to maintain flexibility.
Packet is labeled with yellow colour coding.
Softens rapidly once removed from the packet and handled.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Ligation of small subcutaneous bleeding vessels.
Suturing oral mucosa and mucosal lacerations.
Scrotal skin and prepuce closure in circumcision.

blocks.title: Absorption and properties
bullets: Loses 50% tensile strength in 3 to 5 days, completely gone by 7 to 10 days.
Complete absorption occurs within 60 to 70 days by foreign-body phagocytosis and proteolytic enzymatic digestion.
Provokes intense local tissue inflammation due to its animal protein composition.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Strictly contraindicated in fascial, vascular, or bowel closure due to rapid loss of tensile support.
Manufactured from the submucosa of sheep intestine or serosa of bovine intestine.

viva.q: What is the biological origin of surgical catgut?
viva.a: Submucosa of sheep intestine (ileum) or serosa of cattle intestine, composed of purified natural collagen.

viva.q: By what physiological mechanism is plain catgut absorbed?
viva.a: By enzymatic proteolytic digestion and phagocytosis by tissue macrophages and polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

viva.q: Why is plain catgut unsuitable for abdominal fascial closure?
viva.a: It loses virtually all tensile strength within 7 to 10 days, far before fascial healing can prevent burst abdomen.

image.brief: Sealed yellow packet of plain catgut suture showing foil label details, metric gauge, and amber strand with swaged needle.

items.summary: A natural collagen suture treated with chromium salts to delay enzymatic degradation and prolong mechanical wound support.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Dark brown or olive-green coloured strand.
Supplied sterile in conditioning solution to preserve moisture and pliability.
Dispenser packet is designated by a rich brown colour code.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Suturing episiotomy wounds and perineal lacerations.
Urinary tract and biliary duct closure (does not act as a permanent calculus nidus).
Closure of visceral peritoneum and uterine wall incisions.

blocks.title: Absorption and properties
bullets: Chromium salts tan the collagen molecules, creating cross-links that resist enzymatic cleavage.
Maintains useful tensile strength for 14 to 21 days.
Completely absorbed by phagocytosis within 90 to 120 days.
Produces less tissue reaction than plain catgut but substantially more than synthetic absorbables.

viva.q: Why is catgut treated with chromium salts?
viva.a: Chromium cross-links collagen fibrils, tanning the strand so tissue enzymes take longer to break it down.

viva.q: Why has chromic catgut been widely used in the urinary bladder?
viva.a: It absorbs predictably, preventing the suture from acting as a permanent foreign-body nidus for urinary stone formation.

viva.q: How long does chromic catgut retain tensile strength in living tissue?
viva.a: Approximately 14 to 21 days in healthy vascularized tissue before undergoing significant degradation.

image.brief: Brown packet of sterile chromic catgut suture displaying needle silhouette, metric gauge, and dark brown suture strand.

items.summary: A synthetic braided absorbable copolymer of glycolide and lactide that provides reliable strength and predictable hydrolytic absorption.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Braided multifilament strand, either dyed violet or supplied undyed (white).
Supplied dry in a distinctive violet foil package.
Coated with polyglactin 370 and calcium stearate to ensure smooth tissue transit without chatter.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Gastrointestinal anastomoses (mucosal and seromuscular layers).
Subcutaneous fat and deep dermal approximation.
Ligation of vascular pedicles and mesenteric vessels.
Extra-ocular muscle surgery and pediatric visceral repairs.

blocks.title: Absorption profile
bullets: Retains 75% tensile strength at 2 weeks, 50% at 3 weeks, and roughly 25% at 4 weeks.
Completely absorbed by non-enzymatic chemical hydrolysis within 56 to 70 days.
Causes minimal tissue inflammatory reaction.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Irradiated version (Vicryl Rapide) loses all strength by 7 to 10 days, ideal for skin and episiotomy.
Braided construction has capillary action; avoided in contaminated vascular prostheses.

viva.q: What is the chemical composition of Polyglactin 910?
viva.a: A synthetic copolymer composed of 90% glycolide and 10% L-lactide coated with polyglactin 370 and calcium stearate.

viva.q: By what physiological mechanism is Polyglactin 910 absorbed?
viva.a: By non-enzymatic chemical hydrolysis into glycolic and lactic acids, causing minimal tissue inflammation.

viva.q: How much tensile strength remains at two and three weeks?
viva.a: Roughly 75% tensile strength remains at 2 weeks, and approximately 50% remains at 3 weeks post-implantation.

image.brief: Violet packet of Polyglactin 910 suture showing purple branding, curved needle symbol, and violet braided thread attached.

items.summary: A braided synthetic absorbable homopolymer of glycolic acid that hydrolyses into water and carbon dioxide with low tissue reactivity.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Braided green or beige strand packaged in gold or champagne-coloured foil packets.
Supple multifilament feel with firm knot placement.
May be uncoated or coated with polycaprolate.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: General soft tissue approximation and muscle closure.
Gastrointestinal tract and biliary anastomoses.
Peritoneal closure and ligating pedicles.

blocks.title: Absorption and properties
bullets: Retains 50% tensile strength at 2 to 3 weeks.
Completely absorbed by chemical hydrolysis into glycolic acid within 60 to 90 days.
Historic landmark as the first synthetic absorbable suture introduced into surgery (1970).

viva.q: What was the principal clinical advantage of polyglycolic acid when first invented?
viva.a: It replaced animal-derived catgut with a synthetic material having predictable hydrolytic absorption and minimal antigenicity.

viva.q: How is polyglycolic acid eliminated from the body?
viva.a: Hydrolysed to glycolic acid, which enters the Krebs cycle and is excreted as carbon dioxide and water.

viva.q: Is polyglycolic acid monofilament or braided?
viva.a: It is a braided multifilament suture, giving it high knot security and supple handling.

image.brief: Gold foil packet of polyglycolic acid suture with green braided thread extending from the dispenser.

items.summary: A long-lasting synthetic monofilament absorbable suture formulated for extended wound support in continuous fascial closure.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Smooth monofilament violet or clear strand supplied in a silver-grey foil packet.
Stiff with noticeable handling memory, requiring deliberate knot throws.
Packet is labeled with silver-grey colour coding.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Continuous mass closure of the abdominal wall (rectus sheath and linea alba).
Slow-healing tissues including aponeuroses, tendons, and joint capsules.
Pediatric cardiovascular anastomoses and contaminated laparotomy closure.

blocks.title: Absorption profile
bullets: Unrivalled strength retention among absorbables: 70% at 2 weeks, 50% at 4 weeks, and 25% at 6 weeks.
Complete hydrolytic absorption takes 180 to 210 days (6 to 7 months).
Smooth monofilament surface lacks bacterial capillarity, making it safe in contaminated fields.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: High memory requires 5 to 6 squared throws to guarantee knot stability.
Standard suture for the Jenkins rule of abdominal wall closure (suture length 4 times wound length).

viva.q: Why is polydioxanone preferred for continuous midline abdominal wall closure?
viva.a: It retains tensile strength for up to 6 weeks while its monofilament surface resists bacterial colonization in surgical wounds.

viva.q: How long does polydioxanone take to absorb completely?
viva.a: Approximately 180 to 210 days (around 6 to 7 months) via non-enzymatic chemical hydrolysis.

viva.q: What knot-tying rule must be observed with polydioxanone?
viva.a: Due to high plastic memory, at least 5 to 6 squared throws are needed to prevent knot unraveling.

image.brief: Silver-grey packet of polydioxanone suture showing purple monofilament strand and looped swaged needle.

items.summary: A supple synthetic monofilament absorbable copolymer designed for low-drag subcuticular skin closure with minimal scarring.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Very smooth, flexible monofilament strand, undyed (clear) or dyed violet.
Packaged in a salmon-peach or coral coloured packet.
Substantially softer with far less memory than polydioxanone.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Subcuticular continuous skin closure in abdominal, plastic, and breast surgery.
Soft tissue approximation where tensile stress is minimal.
Bowel anastomoses and urological repairs.

blocks.title: Absorption and properties
bullets: High initial tensile strength that drops rapidly: 50% to 60% at 1 week, 20% to 30% at 2 weeks, negligible by 3 weeks.
Completely absorbed by hydrolysis within 90 to 120 days.
Produces virtually no tissue reaction, leading to fine cosmetic scars.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Because tensile strength drops to near zero by 21 days, it must never be used for high-tension fascial closure.

viva.q: What is the primary cosmetic indication for poliglecaprone 25?
viva.a: Continuous subcuticular skin closure, leaving an aesthetic fine linear scar without stitch marks.

viva.q: Why is poliglecaprone 25 unsuitable for closing abdominal wall fascia?
viva.a: It loses nearly 80% of its strength by 2 weeks, failing to support healing fascia under intra-abdominal pressure.

viva.q: How does handling of poliglecaprone 25 compare with polydioxanone?
viva.a: It is much more pliable, soft, and has far lower memory, tying down easily and smoothly.

image.brief: Salmon-peach packet of poliglecaprone 25 suture showing the clear monofilament strand and cutting needle diagram.

credit.author: Power Dental Group / Techsuture; photographer not identified

items.summary: A natural braided protein suture spun by silkworms, dyed black and waxed, prized for superior handling and knot security.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Braided jet-black thread supplied in a baby-blue foil package.
Completely devoid of memory, extremely supple, and drapes softly.
Ties into exceptionally secure flat knots that do not slip.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Ligation of major blood vessels and deep vascular pedicles.
Seromuscular outer layer of bowel anastomoses (Lembert and Halsted stitches).
Anchoring surgical drains (chest drains, Foley catheters) to skin.
Stay sutures to retract tongue, bladder, or bowel.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Technically classified as non-absorbable, but undergoes slow proteolytic degradation over 1 to 2 years.
Braided capillary structure harbors bacteria; strictly avoided in contaminated or infected wounds.
Avoided in urinary or biliary tract where it acts as a calculus nidus.

viva.q: Why do surgeons value silk for handling and knotting?
viva.a: It has zero memory, high friction coefficient, supreme pliability, and forms flat, reliable knots that rarely slip.

viva.q: Why is surgical silk contraindicated in infected wounds?
viva.a: Its braided multifilament construction exerts capillary action, harboring bacteria away from host macrophages.

viva.q: Is surgical silk permanent inside living human tissue?
viva.a: No, it is slowly degraded by proteolytic enzymes and loses all tensile strength within one to two years.

image.brief: Light blue packet of surgical black braided silk suture with coiled dark thread attached to a curved needle.

items.summary: A synthetic monofilament polyamide suture with high tensile strength and minimal tissue drag, the gold standard for skin closure.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Glossy, smooth black, blue, or clear monofilament strand.
Packaged in a bright green foil packet.
High elastic memory: springs back when uncoiled from the dispenser.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Interrupted, mattress, and continuous cuticular skin closure.
Heavy retention sutures for burst abdomen closure.
Microsurgical neurovascular repairs (fine sizes 8-0 to 10-0).
Corneal and ophthalmic surgery.

blocks.title: Properties
bullets: Non-absorbable, though degrades very slowly by hydrolysis (15% to 20% loss per year).
Completely inert with zero capillarity, minimizing stitch abscesses.
Requires at least 4 to 5 squared throws due to memory.

blocks.title: Removal timing
bullets: Face: 3 to 5 days to avoid stitch marks.
Scalp and neck: 5 to 7 days.
Trunk and abdomen: 7 to 10 days.
Extremities and over joints: 10 to 14 days.

viva.q: Why is monofilament nylon the standard choice for skin suturing?
viva.a: Its smooth inert monofilament body passes without dragging, elicits minimal tissue reaction, and lacks bacterial capillarity.

viva.q: How many throws are required when tying nylon knots?
viva.a: At least four to five throws are needed because the high elastic memory of nylon predisposes knots to slipping.

viva.q: When should facial skin sutures made of nylon be removed?
viva.a: Within 3 to 5 days, to prevent permanent punctate cross-hatching and railway-track epithelial scarring.

image.brief: Bright green foil packet of monofilament polyamide nylon suture showing dark strand and reverse cutting needle symbol.

items.summary: An extremely inert synthetic monofilament suture that retains lifelong tensile strength, standard for vascular and hernia surgery.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Vibrant royal blue or clear monofilament strand.
Packaged in a dark royal blue foil packet.
Slippery surface; exhibits plastic elongation (flattens out when pulled under tension).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Vascular anastomoses (arteriotomies, vein bypass grafts, arteriovenous fistulas).
Fixation of prosthetic hernia mesh in Lichtenstein and incisional repairs.
Abdominal wall fascial mass closure.
Continuous pull-out subcuticular skin closure.

blocks.title: Properties
bullets: Completely non-absorbable; never degrades, hydrolyses, or weakens in tissue.
Lowest thrombogenicity of any suture, critical for blood vessel lumina.
Inert even in the presence of active gross infection.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Requires 5 to 6 throws to ensure knot security.
Never grasp the active strand with forceps or needle holders: crushing creates stress notches that rupture under arterial pulsation.

viva.q: Why is polypropylene mandatory for arterial anastomoses?
viva.a: It retains permanent tensile strength for the patient lifetime, resists degradation, and has the lowest thrombogenicity.

viva.q: What is plastic deformation in polypropylene and why is it useful?
viva.a: Under tension, the strand flattens and locks onto itself, helping secure the knot loops firmly.

viva.q: Why should surgical instruments never clamp the working strand of polypropylene?
viva.a: Serrations cause micro-notches that produce focal stress concentrations, predisposing the suture to rupture under arterial pressure.

image.brief: Dark blue packet of monofilament polypropylene suture with vivid blue thread attached to a double-ended vascular needle.

items.summary: A metallic 316L alloy wire delivering immense mechanical strength and complete biological inertness for bone and sternal closure.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Polished silver metallic wire, supplied as single monofilament or twisted multifilament strands.
Rigid, metallic feel; heavy foil or blister packaging with yellow or metallic labels.
Sizes designated by Brown and Sharpe (B&S) wire gauge (sizes 18 to 40) or standard metric.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Closure of median sternotomy following cardiac and thoracic operations.
Orthopaedic fixation: tension-band wiring of patella and olecranon fractures.
Mass abdominal closure or retention sutures in severe burst abdomen.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Kinking creates metal fatigue, causing sudden wire fracture under stress.
Sharp cut wire ends can puncture gloves or erode through skin causing chronic pain.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Secured by crossing and twisting the two ends using wire twister forceps rather than tying standard knots.

viva.q: What is the primary surgical use of stainless steel wire in cardiothoracic surgery?
viva.a: Rigid approximation and re-apposition of the split sternum following median sternotomy.

viva.q: What is the primary mechanism of wire suture failure?
viva.a: Kinking or acute bending during handling induces metal fatigue, leading to wire snapping under cyclic respiratory stress.

viva.q: What grade of steel is used for surgical wire?
viva.a: Medical-grade 316L stainless steel with low carbon content, chromium, nickel, and molybdenum to prevent corrosion.

image.brief: Shiny stainless steel wire suture with heavy swaged cutting needle beside wire twister forceps on a sterile tray.

items.summary: A strong braided synthetic non-absorbable suture coated with polybutilate or silicone, providing permanent tensile strength for valve and tendon surgery.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Braided green or white thread supplied in an orange-coloured package.
Coated with polybutilate or silicone to reduce friction and tissue drag.
Very high tensile strength with soft, pliable handling.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Prosthetic cardiac valve replacement (mitral and aortic annuloplasty rings and valves).
Tendon and ligament repairs (Achilles tendon repair, rotator cuff reconstruction).
Cervical cerclage (McDonald or Shirodkar tape/suture) in obstetrics.

blocks.title: Properties
bullets: Completely non-absorbable; maintains lifelong tensile strength without degrading in tissue.
Braided structure provides excellent knot security.
Avoided in contaminated fields due to bacterial harboring within braided interstices.

viva.q: Why is braided polyester preferred for prosthetic heart valve seating?
viva.a: It delivers permanent high tensile strength, supreme fatigue resistance, and locks knots securely against dynamic pulsatile cardiac strain.

viva.q: What coating is applied to polyester sutures and why?
viva.a: Coated with polybutilate or silicone to lubricate the braid, ensuring smooth passage through dense fibrous annuli without sawing.

viva.q: What colour packet designates polyester sutures?
viva.a: Packaged in an orange-coloured foil dispenser.

image.brief: Orange foil packet of braided green polyester suture with double-ended pledgetted needles on a cardiac tray.

items.summary: A curved needle with a circular cross-section that tapers to a sharp point, piercing soft tissues without slicing their fibers.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Shaft has a smooth circular cross-section with no cutting edges.
Tapers smoothly to a sharp conical point.
Symbolized on the suture packet by a solid black circle.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Suturing hollow gastrointestinal organs (stomach, small bowel, colon).
Peritoneum, urinary bladder, ureters, and biliary ducts.
Blood vessels and vascular anastomoses (prevents leakage from cut tracts).
Subcutaneous fat and parenchymal organs like liver and kidney.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Pushes tissue fibers apart rather than cutting them; the tissue then contracts snugly around the suture strand.
Never used on tough fibrous tissue like skin or fascia because forcing a round needle bends the shaft and tears the tissue.

viva.q: What symbol on a suture packet denotes a round-bodied needle?
viva.a: A solid filled circle symbol.

viva.q: Why is a round-bodied needle chosen for bowel anastomosis?
viva.a: It separates mucosal and muscular fibers without cutting them, producing a leak-proof seal around the thread.

viva.q: Why is a round-bodied needle avoided for suturing skin?
viva.a: Skin dermis consists of dense collagen bundles that resist puncture; forcing a round needle causes bending or crude tearing.

image.brief: Curved round-bodied surgical needle held in a needle holder showing circular shaft geometry and sharp conical point.

items.summary: Needles with triangular cross-sections possessing three sharp edges designed to slice through tough, dense fibrous tissues like skin and fascia.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Triangular cross-section with three sharp cutting edges.
Conventional cutting needle has its third edge on the inner concave curve (upward-pointing triangle symbol).
Reverse cutting needle has its third edge on the outer convex curve (downward-pointing inverted triangle symbol).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Suturing skin, subcuticular dermis, tough deep fascia, and aponeurosis.
Suturing tendon sheaths, joint capsules, and tough fibrous scars.

blocks.title: Why reverse cutting is superior for skin
bullets: The flat inner curve rests against the wound margin, distributing pull tension broadly.
Conventional cutting places a sharp apex along the line of tension, predisposing the suture to slice out through the skin edge.

viva.q: What is the structural difference between conventional cutting and reverse cutting needles?
viva.a: Conventional cutting has its third sharp edge on the inner concave curve; reverse cutting places it on the outer convex curve.

viva.q: Why is reverse cutting preferred for skin closure?
viva.a: The flat inner curve prevents the suture thread from slicing through the wound edge when tension is applied.

viva.q: What packet symbol indicates a reverse cutting needle?
viva.a: An inverted triangle with the apex pointing downwards.

image.brief: Diagram of conventional cutting and reverse cutting triangular profiles beside an actual curved reverse cutting skin needle.

items.summary: A surgical needle manufactured with the suture strand crimped directly into a drilled hole at its base, eliminating tissue drag and trauma.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Needle and suture form a single continuous unit without an open eye or hole.
The strand emerges seamlessly from a precision-drilled bore at the base of the needle.
Diameter of the needle shank matches the caliber of the attached suture thread.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Truly atraumatic: only a single strand passes through the puncture tract, avoiding tissue tearing.
Eliminates the bulky doubled loop of thread seen with eyed needles.
Supplied factory-sterilised and sharp for every pass; no time wasted threading needles.

blocks.title: Varieties
bullets: Permanently swaged: thread remains firmly bonded until intentionally cut.
Controlled release (pop-off): detaches with a quick straight tug, ideal for interrupted deep sutures.

viva.q: Why is a swaged needle termed atraumatic?
viva.a: The needle diameter matches the suture thread, so a single strand passes through the puncture hole without creating a larger tear.

viva.q: What is a control-release (pop-off) swaged needle?
viva.a: A needle designed to release cleanly from the suture with a straight pull, speeding up interrupted suturing.

viva.q: What are two major disadvantages of traditional eyed needles?
viva.a: They pull a doubled suture loop that tears tissue tracts, require manual threading, and dull with repeated autoclaving.

image.brief: Close-up photograph of the crimped base of an atraumatic swaged needle where the suture thread seamlessly emerges.

items.summary: A long straight needle with a sharp cutting tip held directly in the fingers without a needle holder for rapid skin closure.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Straight cylindrical steel needle (5 to 10 cm long) devoid of any curvature.
Ends in a sharp cutting or reverse cutting triangular tip.
Supplied with a swaged suture strand or traditional eye.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Rapid closure of long abdominal laparotomy incisions.
Placing subcuticular skin sutures along linear wounds.
Tendon suturing (Bunnell and Kessler repairs).

blocks.title: Technique and complications
bullets: Manipulated directly between the thumb and forefingers of the dominant hand.
High risk of sharp needle-stick injuries and glove punctures due to proximity of fingers to the sharp point.

viva.q: How is a straight Keith needle manipulated during surgery?
viva.a: Held directly with the fingers without employing a needle holder.

viva.q: What is the primary danger associated with using straight needles?
viva.a: Increased frequency of glove punctures and accidental needle-stick injuries to the surgeon and assistant.

viva.q: Where is a straight Keith needle primarily utilized?
viva.a: Rapid hand suturing of extensive abdominal skin incisions and linear subcuticular closures.

image.brief: Straight Keith needle shown next to a standard curved needle on a surgical ruler showing its 7 cm length.

items.summary: A curved needle with a rounded blunt tip designed to dissect parenchymal organs without puncturing fragile blood vessels.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Curved needle whose tip is rounded and blunt rather than sharp.
Packaged with a symbol showing an open circle with a rounded point.
Cannot puncture intact skin or glove easily.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Suturing fragile parenchymal organs like the liver and spleen (liver laceration repair).
Uterine wall suturing in caesarean delivery.
Fascial closure in patients with high-risk blood-borne viral infections (HIV, Hepatitis B/C) to eliminate sharp needle sticks.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Pushes parenchymal vessels aside instead of lacerating them, preventing intra-parenchymal hematomas.
Significantly reduces occupational glove perforation rates in the operating theatre.

viva.q: Why is a blunt taperpoint needle used to suture the liver?
viva.a: Its blunt tip pushes fragile intrahepatic bile ducts and blood vessels aside without tearing them, preventing hemorrhage.

viva.q: What role do blunt needles play in operating theatre occupational safety?
viva.a: They prevent accidental percutaneous needle-stick injuries to surgical personnel during fascial closure.

viva.q: Can a blunt needle penetrate intact adult skin?
viva.a: No, its rounded tip cannot pierce the dense stratum corneum and dermis of intact human skin.

image.brief: Curved blunt taperpoint surgical needle showing its rounded non-sharp tip held in a needle holder.

items.summary: A fundamental two-throw surgical knot formed by reversing direction on successive half-hitches to create a balanced, non-slipping lock.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Two symmetrical interlocking half-hitches.
Both free ends emerge parallel to their respective standing strands.
Lies completely flat against the approximated tissue without twisting.

blocks.title: Steps of construction
bullets: First throw: cross strands (left over right) and pull flat with equal horizontal tension.
Second throw: cross strands in the reverse direction (right over left) and snug down flat.
Maintain equal tension on both strands to prevent the knot from spilling into a slip knot.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: If the second throw is tied in the same direction, an insecure granny knot results.
Additional third and fourth throws are added to lock modern synthetic sutures.

viva.q: What defines a true square (reef) knot?
viva.a: Two consecutive single throws tied in opposite directions with equal tension, allowing the loops to interlock symmetrically and lie flat.

viva.q: What error produces a granny knot instead of a square knot?
viva.a: Failing to reverse the direction of the hands on the second throw, tying both half-hitches in identical orientation.

viva.q: What happens if unequal tension is applied to the two strands?
viva.a: The knot flips into an insecure slip knot (half-hitch) that slides along the standing strand.

image.brief: Illustration of an interlocking square reef knot with strands lying parallel and flat against a tissue plane.

items.summary: A modified square knot with a double-wrapped initial throw that provides friction resistance to prevent slipping under tension.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: First throw features two loops (double twist) through the eye of the knot.
Second throw is a single reversed throw tied square over the first.
Bulkier than a simple reef knot.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Approximating tissues under tension (such as rectus sheath or deep fascia).
Tying slippery monofilament materials like nylon and polypropylene.
Vascular pedicle ligation where maintaining tension during knotting is crucial.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages
bullets: Double twist generates friction that holds the tissue approximated while the second throw is placed.
Bulkier knot volume increases foreign body mass; increased friction makes snugging down in deep cavities difficult.

viva.q: What is the defining feature of a surgeons knot?
viva.a: A double wrap on the initial throw followed by a single reversed throw to lock it.

viva.q: When is a surgeons knot indicated over a simple square knot?
viva.a: When closing wound layers under mechanical tension or using slippery monofilament sutures that tend to spring open.

viva.q: What is the disadvantage of using surgeons knots routinely in delicate viscera?
viva.a: Increased knot bulk that elicits foreign body reaction and difficulty sliding the knot down into deep cavities.

image.brief: Diagram showing the double wrap of the base loop locked by a single flat counter-throw in a surgeons knot.

items.summary: An erroneous asymmetrical surgical knot formed when consecutive throws are made in the same direction, notorious for slipping under tension.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Asymmetric knot where the free ends emerge at right angles to the loop rather than lying flat.
Knot cocks sideways and slips readily when pulled.
Produced when the surgeon fails to reverse direction between the first and second throws.

blocks.title: Dangers in surgery
bullets: Prone to spontaneous slippage and unraveling under physiological tissue tension.
Can cause catastrophic slippage of vascular ligatures with secondary hemorrhage.
Causes early dehiscence of fascial layers and abdominal wound burst.

blocks.title: Prevention
bullets: Always cross hands or reverse loop orientation deliberately on each subsequent throw.
Verify that every throw squares down flat before applying the next lock.

viva.q: Why is a granny knot dangerous in surgery?
viva.a: It lacks friction locking and slips under wound tension, risking fatal ligature blow-off or fascial dehiscence.

viva.q: How does a granny knot form accidentally?
viva.a: By repeating the same direction of throwing twice consecutively instead of reversing the second throw.

viva.q: How can you visually distinguish a granny knot from a square knot?
viva.a: In a granny knot, the suture tails cock out perpendicularly, whereas in a square knot, the tails lie flat and parallel.

image.brief: Diagram highlighting the asymmetrical twisted loops and perpendicular strand exit of an unstable granny knot.

items.summary: A knot-tying technique utilizing the tip of a needle holder to loop and grasp short suture ends, conserving material in confined spaces.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: The needle holder beak is placed over the long standing strand, looped once or twice, and then grasps the short suture tail.
The short tail is pulled through the loop and laid flat in the opposite direction.
Successive throws alternate looping over and under the standing strand.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Routine cutaneous skin suturing.
Confined or deep anatomical spaces where surgeon fingers cannot reach.
Tying when short suture tails remain, preventing waste of expensive suture materials.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Only the short cut tail should be grasped with the needle holder jaws.
Never grasp the standing active monofilament strand, which induces micro-crush fracture.

viva.q: What is the primary advantage of an instrument tie?
viva.a: It conserves suture thread by working with short ends and enables knot tying in deep, narrow surgical spaces.

viva.q: Why must the needle holder never grasp the standing monofilament strand during an instrument tie?
viva.a: The serrated metal jaws crush and weaken the synthetic strand, causing premature breakage.

viva.q: How is a square knot ensured during an instrument tie?
viva.a: By alternating the direction of wrapping the strand around the needle holder on successive throws.

image.brief: Surgeon hands demonstrating an instrument tie: needle holder jaws looping around suture and grasping the short tail.

items.summary: A sterile disposable handheld device delivering rectangular stainless steel staples to close skin wounds, paired with a specialized extractor.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Pistol-grip or squeeze plastic applicator preloaded with 316L medical stainless steel staples.
Transparent cartridge displays remaining staple count.
Staple remover features two lower horizontal prongs and a central upper descending wedge.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Rapid skin closure of extensive incisions: laparotomy, caesarean section, orthopaedic joint replacement, and scalp wounds.
Staple remover painlessly extracts healed staples at 7 to 14 days.

blocks.title: Steps of application and removal
bullets: Application: assistant everts skin edges with toothed forceps; surgeon aligns arrow over cut and squeezes fully to form a rectangular staple.
Extraction: lower prongs slide under staple bridge; squeezing handles pushes central bar down, pivoting prongs outward for vertical withdrawal.

viva.q: What is the main clinical advantage of skin staplers over manual suturing?
viva.a: Significant reduction in operative closure time and lower risk of wound contamination from needle punctures.

viva.q: Why must skin edges be everted with forceps before firing a staple?
viva.a: Eversion counteracts natural inward rolling of skin, ensuring proper epidermal apposition and a narrow cosmetic scar.

viva.q: How does the staple extractor remove staples without tissue tearing?
viva.a: It depresses the middle of the staple bridge, causing both pointed ends to rotate outwards and withdraw along their entry tracts.

image.brief: Disposable plastic skin stapler with transparent cartridge showing steel staples alongside a metallic staple remover tool.

items.summary: A surgical stapler that places two double-staggered rows of titanium staples while simultaneously dividing tissue between them with an internal blade.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Two-piece interlocking metallic instrument: an anvil arm and a cartridge arm containing staple reloads.
Features a central sliding firing knob that drives a sharp integrated knife blade between staple rows.
Cartridges are colour-coded for tissue thickness (vascular white, regular bowel blue, thick stomach green).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Creating side-to-side (functional end-to-end) gastrointestinal anastomoses.
Transection of stomach, small intestine, and colon during resections.
Lung wedge resection and lobectomy in thoracic surgery.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Staple line bleeding from divided submucosal vessels.
Anastomotic leakage or dehiscence if cartridge height is mismatched to tissue thickness.

viva.q: What two actions are performed simultaneously by a linear cutter stapler?
viva.a: It applies two parallel staggered rows of titanium staples on either side while an integrated blade divides the tissue in between.

viva.q: What do different cartridge colours signify in surgical staplers?
viva.a: Cartridge colours designate closed staple height tailored for specific tissue thicknesses (white for vascular, blue for bowel, green for stomach).

viva.q: Name two operations where a linear cutter stapler is routinely utilized.
viva.a: Side-to-side ileocolic anastomosis following right hemicolectomy and distal gastrectomy.

image.brief: Linear cutter stapler shown separated into cartridge and anvil halves with a blue bowel cartridge seated in the jaw.

items.summary: A cylindrical surgical instrument that applies a circular double row of titanium staples and cores out tissue to create an inverted visceral anastomosis.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Curved or straight tubular shaft with a circular cartridge head and a detachable circular anvil mounted on a central trocar.
Rotating wing-nut at the base adjusts tissue compression gap, indicated by a green safety window.
Heavy firing trigger handle with a safety release lock.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Colorectal end-to-end anastomosis in low anterior resection (LAR) for rectal cancer.
Esophagojejunal anastomosis after total gastrectomy.
Transanal hemorrhoidal dearterialization or stapled hemorrhoidopexy (PPH).

blocks.title: Steps and safety check
bullets: Purse-string suture secures anvil in proximal lumen; trocar penetrates distal stump to dock into anvil.
Turn wing-nut until indicator enters green zone; release safety lock and fire trigger.
Gently withdraw instrument; immediately inspect both cut donuts of tissue.
Checking that both excised rings (donuts) are complete and intact confirms an unbroken, full-thickness circumferential seal.

viva.q: What is the clinical significance of inspecting tissue donuts after firing an EEA stapler?
viva.a: Two complete continuous donuts confirm that full-thickness bowel was incorporated into the staple line around the entire circumference.

viva.q: What action must be taken if a donut has an incomplete gap?
viva.a: The anastomosis is incomplete and leaky; it must be reinforced with interrupted sutures or protected with a proximal diverting stoma.

viva.q: In which colorectal operation is the circular stapler indispensable?
viva.a: Low anterior resection (LAR), enabling ultra-low colorectal anastomosis deep in the pelvis where manual suturing is impossible.

image.brief: Curved intraluminal circular stapler showing the cylindrical cartridge, attached circular anvil, and gap indicator window.

items.summary: A knitted non-absorbable monofilament polypropylene sheet used to reinforce weakened abdominal wall fascia in tension-free hernia repairs.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Porous, knitted flexible sheet of translucent white or blue polypropylene monofilament.
Features distinctive two-way mechanical stretch and large pore size (> 1 mm).
Supplied sterile in flat rectangular sheets (e.g., 7.5 x 15 cm or 15 x 15 cm).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Lichtenstein tension-free repair of inguinal hernia.
Onlay, sublay (Rives-Stoppa), or preperitoneal repair of ventral and incisional hernias.
Femoral hernia and umbilical hernia repairs.

blocks.title: Biological incorporation and safety
bullets: Large pores permit rapid macrophage migration to eliminate bacteria and allow robust fibrovascular collagen ingrowth.
Strictly contraindicated in direct contact with intraperitoneal bowel: causes severe adhesions, visceral erosion, and enterocutaneous fistula.

viva.q: What is the principle of Lichtenstein tension-free hernia repair?
viva.a: Reinforcing the weakened transversalis fascia of the inguinal canal floor with prosthetic mesh without pulling muscular edges under tension.

viva.q: Why must large-pore (> 1 mm) mesh be chosen over dense microporous mesh?
viva.a: Large pores allow macrophages to clear bacterial contaminants and promote vigorous collagen ingrowth that incorporates the prosthesis.

viva.q: What catastrophic complication occurs if bare polypropylene mesh touches the intestine?
viva.a: Dense fibrous adhesions leading to bowel wall erosion, chronic obstruction, and enterocutaneous fistula formation.

image.brief: Rectangular sheet of knitted translucent polypropylene hernia mesh showing open porous weave pattern on a sterile drape.

items.summary: A two-sided prosthetic mesh featuring a porous synthetic side for fascial ingrowth and a smooth anti-adhesive barrier side facing the viscera.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Distinct dual-sided sheet: one side is rough porous white mesh (polypropylene or polyester), the other side is a shiny, smooth anti-adhesive layer.
Anti-adhesive barrier consists of oxidized regenerated cellulose, collagen, omega-3 fatty acids, or ePTFE.
Often includes alignment orientation marks printed on the barrier surface.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Laparoscopic intraperitoneal onlay mesh (IPOM) repair of ventral, umbilical, and incisional hernias.
Placed directly inside the peritoneal cavity in immediate contact with visceral loops.

blocks.title: Mechanism and precautions
bullets: The rough parietal surface incorporates securely into the muscular anterior abdominal wall.
The smooth visceral barrier prevents peritoneal fibrinous adhesion formation during the critical 1 to 2 week mesothelial healing window.
Must be positioned with the smooth barrier facing the bowel; accidental reversal induces dense intestinal adhesions.

viva.q: What is the rationale for a dual-sided composite mesh in intraperitoneal repair?
viva.a: The parietal porous surface incorporates with the abdominal wall, while the visceral barrier prevents intestinal adhesions and fistulization.

viva.q: Which surface must face the abdominal viscera?
viva.a: The smooth anti-adhesive barrier surface must always face toward the abdominal viscera and intestine.

viva.q: What materials compose the anti-adhesive visceral layer?
viva.a: Absorbable collagen, oxidized regenerated cellulose, omega-3 fatty acids, or expanded polytetrafluoroethylene.

image.brief: Composite IPOM mesh showing contrasting surfaces: porous white parietal mesh backing and shiny translucent visceral barrier face.

title.en: Absorbable gelatin sponge and oxidized cellulose

items.summary: Porous resorbable biomaterials applied to raw oozing tissue surfaces to provide a physical matrix that accelerates local clot formation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Absorbable gelatin sponge is a dry, off-white, light, pliable, porous sponge pad.
Oxidized regenerated cellulose appears as a sterile off-white knitted fabric or gauze strip with a faint caramel scent.
Both can be trimmed with scissors to conform to the bleeding surgical bed.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Controlling persistent venous or capillary oozing from the liver bed after cholecystectomy or partial hepatectomy.
Haemostasis in presacral pelvic venous bleeding and prostatic beds.
Neurosurgical cavities and spinal cord dural margins.
Tooth socket and oral mucosal oozing in coagulopathic patients.

blocks.title: Mechanism and absorption
bullets: Provides a physical structural scaffold that traps platelets, induces mechanical tamponade, and accelerates intrinsic clotting.
Completely absorbed in vivo within 4 to 6 weeks with negligible foreign-body scarring.
Must be removed from confined bony canals or spinal cord spaces once haemostasis is secure to prevent compressive swelling.

viva.q: How does absorbable gelatin sponge stop capillary oozing?
viva.a: It acts as a physical matrix that traps blood, promotes platelet aggregation, and stabilizes the fibrin clot at the bleeding surface.

viva.q: How long does it take for topical gelatin or oxidized cellulose to be resorbed in vivo?
viva.a: Completely resorbed through enzymatic phagocytosis in 4 to 6 weeks without leaving a permanent foreign body.

viva.q: Why should topical haemostatics be removed from enclosed bony spaces?
viva.a: The material swells upon hydration, creating pressure that can cause ischemic neurological compression in narrow canals.

image.brief: Sterile dry porous gelatin sponge square alongside a strip of oxidized regenerated cellulose mesh on a surgical tray.
